title: Assess the quality of citrus for export

lessons.title: The citrus export industry, terms and requirements
lessons.html:
Background and structure

Citrus is South Africa's largest fresh fruit export, and the country is one of the world's biggest exporters of fresh citrus. Production is spread across Limpopo, Mpumalanga, the Eastern Cape (Sundays River Valley, Patensie and Kat River), the Western Cape (Citrusdal and Clanwilliam), KwaZulu-Natal and the Northern Cape along the Orange River. Main markets include Europe, the UK, the Middle East, Russia, Asia, China and the USA.

The Citrus Growers' Association of Southern Africa (CGA) represents growers, and Citrus Research International (CRI) carries out research on pests, diseases and post-harvest handling. The chain runs from growers to packhouses, cold stores, exporters, ports and shipping lines to importers and retailers.

Citrus types and terminology

  • Oranges: navels (early season) and Valencias (late season).
  • Soft citrus: mandarins, clementines and satsumas, easy-peelers.
  • Lemons and limes, and grapefruit such as Star Ruby.
  • Count: number of fruit per carton related to fruit diameter.
  • Rind colour: measured against colour charts; degreening with ethylene may be used to improve colour where allowed.
  • Juice content, TSS, acid and TSS:acid ratio: key internal maturity measures.
  • Blemish: any mark on the rind; class tolerances limit blemish area and type.

Legislative and logistical requirements

Citrus exports are regulated under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990, with PPECB doing export inspections and cold chain oversight under the PPECB Act 9 of 1983. Phytosanitary requirements are particularly important for citrus. Markets such as the EU have strict rules on pests and diseases like false codling moth (FCM) and citrus black spot (CBS), and some markets require cold treatment or a systems approach that combines orchard controls, packhouse controls and inspections.

Compliance means: orchards and packhouses registered for each market, pest and disease monitoring in the orchard, correct post-harvest treatments within residue limits, correct carton marking, and presentation of the consignment with all documents.

lessons.title: Sampling and judging external quality
lessons.html:
Selecting a representative sample

  • Use the sample size in the export standards for the consignment.
  • Select cartons at random from different pallets and positions.
  • Check that cultivar, count, class and codes on each carton match its contents.
  • Record pallet and carton identification.

External quality checks

  • Size: fruit diameter within the declared count; use sizing rings or callipers.
  • Rind colour: compare with the colour chart for the type and market; colour requirements differ for navels, soft citrus, lemons and grapefruit.
  • Shape: typical of the cultivar; misshapen fruit or large navel ends may be limited.
  • Rind texture: smooth, firm rind; coarse or puffy fruit may fail.
  • Blemishes and damage (see the next lesson).
  • Decay: green and blue mould (Penicillium), sour rot and other rots.
  • Pests: live insects, scale, mealybug and any sign of FCM or fruit fly.
  • Wax and fungicide application: even coverage and no residue streaks.
  • Packing: correct fill, no loose fruit, carton strength and stacking.

Each defect is counted and expressed as a percentage of fruit in the sample. Class 1 has the lowest tolerances, and the main markets usually require Class 1. Some defects, such as decay and quarantine pests, have very low or zero tolerances because they can spread or close a market.

Good light is essential. Inspect on a clean, well-lit table, turning every fruit so that the whole rind is seen, including the stem end and the navel or stylar end.

Recording your results

Record defects per carton on the inspection sheet, separating cosmetic blemishes from serious defects such as decay and pests. Note the count and colour reading for each carton. Where a defect is borderline, measure the affected area against the tolerance described in the standard rather than guessing. Accurate records allow the packhouse to trace a problem back to a specific orchard block or packing line.

lessons.title: Common external abnormalities and non-conformities
lessons.html:
Recognising citrus abnormalities

A citrus assessor must recognise the common rind problems and know which are cosmetic and which are serious. The main groups are:

Mechanical and environmental damage

  • Wind scar: grey or silvery scarring where fruit rubbed against branches.
  • Hail damage: healed dents or scars from hail.
  • Sunburn: yellow, hard or bleached patches on the sun-exposed side.
  • Oleocellosis (oil spotting): green or brown spots caused by oil released from rind glands when turgid fruit is handled roughly, often in the early morning.
  • Bruises, cuts and punctures: from picking, clippers or rough handling; fresh wounds lead to mould.
  • Long stems: stems not clipped short can puncture neighbouring fruit.

Pest damage

  • Thrips scarring: ring-shaped scarring around the stem end.
  • Scale insects and mealybug on the rind or under the calyx.
  • FCM damage: small entry holes with brown discolouration; this is a phytosanitary concern for many markets.
  • Fruit fly stings.

Diseases

  • Citrus black spot (CBS): dark lesions on the rind; a quarantine disease for certain markets.
  • Green and blue mould and other decays.
  • Melanose and other cosmetic fungal marks.

Physiological disorders

  • Creasing: grooves in the rind from weak albedo.
  • Puffiness: rind separating from the flesh, common in some soft citrus.
  • Rind breakdown and pitting after storage, sometimes linked to chilling or water loss.
  • Navel end splitting in navels.

When you find a suspected quarantine pest or disease, record it carefully, keep the fruit for identification if the procedure requires, and report it to the responsible inspector or supervisor. Do not guess or ignore it.

lessons.title: Internal quality, cold chain and the outcome
lessons.html:
Internal quality

Citrus is non-climacteric. It does not get sweeter after harvest, so it must be mature when picked. Internal tests on a set number of fruit include:

  • Juice content: juice extracted and expressed as a percentage of fruit mass.
  • TSS (Brix): with a refractometer.
  • Acid: by titration.
  • TSS:acid ratio: calculated; it indicates taste balance.
  • Internal checks for granulation (dry segments), seeds where seedlessness is claimed, and internal decay or larvae.

Results are compared with the minimum requirements for the type, cultivar and market.

Cold chain regimes

Citrus generally stores longer than stone fruit, but it is still vulnerable to decay, water loss and, in some types, chilling injury. Some markets require cold treatment against FCM or fruit fly: fruit is held at or below a prescribed pulp temperature for a prescribed number of days, monitored with calibrated probes in the container or ship. If the temperature rises above the limit, the treatment may fail and have to be restarted or extended.

The assessor monitors pulp temperatures before loading, probe calibration and placement for cold treatment, container set points against instructions, and cold store records.

Determining the outcome

  1. Check that internal quality meets the maturity standard.
  2. Calculate defect and decay percentages against class tolerances.
  3. Check phytosanitary findings: any quarantine pest or disease finding for that market is serious.
  4. Check packing, marking and registration.
  5. Decide to pass, downgrade or reject for the market, and record reasons.

A consignment that fails for one market because of a phytosanitary issue may still be acceptable for another market with different requirements, if the rules allow.

Key points

  • Citrus is South Africa's largest fresh fruit export; the CGA and CRI support the industry.
  • Phytosanitary pests and diseases such as FCM and CBS are critical for market access.
  • Know the difference between cosmetic blemishes and serious defects.
  • Citrus is non-climacteric and must be mature when picked.
  • Cold treatment protocols must be monitored with calibrated probes.
